sections.title: The wettest address on Earth
sections.intro_md:
In the twelve months from August 1860 to July 1861, a rain gauge at Cherrapunji, now called **Sohra**, collected **26,461 mm** of rain. That is 26 metres of water, enough to drown a nine-storey building, and it is still the world record for a single year. In July 1861 alone it caught 9,300 mm, about eleven times what Delhi gets in a whole year.

Sixteen kilometres west, the village of **Mawsynram** now claims the title of wettest inhabited place, with an average near **11,900 mm** a year. The reason is a wall. Warm, wet air off the Bay of Bengal crosses the flat plains of Bangladesh, hits the southern cliffs of the Shillong Plateau and is forced up 1,400 m in a few kilometres. It cools, and drops almost everything it carries.

The paradox: Sohra runs short of drinking water every winter. The rain runs off thin soil into deep gorges, and from November to February the plateau dries out. This is the place the geographer S. P. Chatterjee named in 1936: **Meghalaya**, the abode of clouds.

spotlights.name: Mawsynram
spotlights.spot_it: A village on the southern edge of the plateau, about 1,400 m up, usually inside a cloud.
spotlights.story_md: Mawsynram's long-run average is about 11,872 mm a year, and the Guinness book lists 26,000 mm for 1985. Two towns in Colombia, Lloró and López de Micay, report even higher averages from shorter, less certain records, so the crown is contested. Life adapts. Farmers and cowherds in the southern Khasi Hills have long worn the **knup**, a full-body hood of woven bamboo and leaves that covers the back like a turtle shell and leaves both hands free. Roads are cut into the cliff, and houses are roofed in tin that roars through the monsoon.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The world's rainfall extreme is a real, lived address in India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Mawsynram: where an umbrella is something you wear like a shell.

spotlights.name: Sohra (Cherrapunji)
spotlights.spot_it: Bare grassy plateau on top, dense forest in the gorges below, cloud in between.
spotlights.story_md: The British called it Cherrapunji, a Bengali name meaning roughly a cluster of villages around Cherra. The Khasi name is **Sohra**, and the state uses it again. Its record of 26,461 mm in one year and 9,300 mm in July 1861 still stands. The average is close to 11,800 mm. Yet the plateau top is almost treeless grassland: forest was cleared long ago, the topsoil washed away, and the rock below holds little water. In the dry months women queue at springs. A place drowned in summer and thirsty in winter is the best short lesson in how soil, not rain alone, decides water.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that water security depends on storage and soil, not just rainfall.
spotlights.memory_hook: 26 metres of rain in a year, and still a queue at the spring in January.

sections.title: Meghalaya at a glance
sections.intro_md:
Meghalaya is a high, green rectangle tucked between Assam to the north and **Bangladesh** to the south and west, with about 440 km of international border. It covers **22,429 km²**, about 0.7% of India, and had **29,66,889** people in Census 2011.

It is the home of three main peoples. The **Khasi** and the closely related **Pnar** (Jaintia) live in the east and centre; the **Garo**, who call themselves **A·chik**, live in the west. Scheduled Tribes make up about 86% of the population. About **74.6%** are Christian, one of only three Christian-majority states in India, alongside Mizoram and Nagaland.

Three facts make it unusual in India. Property and clan names pass through women. Two of its three main languages belong to different language families that split thousands of years ago. And it became a state not through violence but through a long, peaceful hill-state movement, gaining autonomy in 1970 and full statehood on **21 January 1972**. Its capital, **Shillong**, had been the capital of all of Assam for almost a century before that.

spotlights.name: Shillong
spotlights.when: Capital of Assam 1874 to 1972; of Meghalaya since
spotlights.spot_it: Pine ridges, tin roofs in every colour, steep lanes and traffic jams at 1,500 m.
spotlights.story_md: Shillong takes its name from **U Shyllong**, a deity believed to live on Shillong Peak, which at about 1,965 m is the highest point in the state. The British made it the headquarters of the new Assam province in 1874, and it stayed the capital of a much larger Assam until Meghalaya split off. The rolling pine hills reminded colonial officers of Scotland, and the nickname 'Scotland of the East' stuck. A nine-hole golf course came in 1898 and an 18-hole course in 1924. The 2011 census counted about 1.43 lakh people in the city proper; the wider urban area is much bigger.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One city has been the political centre of the whole north-east for 150 years.
spotlights.memory_hook: A god on the peak, a golf course in the valley, and a Scottish nickname.

sections.title: The land: a plateau of cliffs, gorges and caves
sections.intro_md:
Meghalaya sits on the **Shillong Plateau**, a block of very old rock, more than a billion years old in places, that has been pushed up between the Brahmaputra valley and the Bangladesh plains. In 1897 one of the largest earthquakes ever recorded lifted part of it by around 11 m in seconds.

The plateau tilts. In the north it slopes gently toward Assam. In the south it ends in cliffs that drop up to 1,000 m to the plains, and that edge is where the rain falls, the rivers cut gorges and the waterfalls plunge. The south is also limestone country. Rain, slightly acidic, has eaten the rock into an estimated **500 caves**, including the longest in South Asia.

In the west the Garo Hills are lower and warmer, with the Nokrek ridge at 1,412 m. In the centre are the Khasi Hills, with the highest ground around Shillong. In the east the Jaintia Hills roll toward Assam's Barak valley. Everywhere, water decides the shape of the land.

spotlights.name: Nohkalikai Falls
spotlights.spot_it: A single ribbon of water falling off a plateau edge into a green pool far below.
spotlights.story_md: At **340 m**, Nohkalikai is the tallest plunge waterfall in India: the water falls clear of the rock the whole way. The pool at the bottom is an unusual green. The name means 'the leap of Ka Likai'. In the legend, a widowed porter named Likai remarried. Jealous of her love for her daughter, the new husband killed the child and cooked her. Likai came home starving, ate the meal, then found a finger in the betel basket, understood, and ran off the cliff. In the dry months, December to February, the fall thins to a trickle.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the plateau's edge made visible, and a story every Khasi child knows.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ka Likai's leap: 340 m and the darkest folktale on the plateau.

spotlights.name: The Umngot river at Dawki
spotlights.spot_it: Boats that seem to hover in the air over a riverbed you can see 5 m down.
spotlights.story_md: The Umngot leaves the plateau at **Dawki**, a border town where a road crosses into Bangladesh. In the dry season it runs so clear that photos of boats look faked: the hull floats over pebbles that are plainly visible metres below. The clarity comes from a small, forested catchment with little silt in winter. In the monsoon the same river turns brown and fast. The suspension bridge at Dawki was built by the British in 1932. On the far bank lies Jaflong in Bangladesh, where stone is quarried from the same riverbed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the best-known image of Meghalaya on Indian social media.
spotlights.memory_hook: A boat floating on air, with Bangladesh on the far bank.

spotlights.name: Mawsmai and the show caves of Sohra
spotlights.spot_it: A lit limestone passage where you squeeze sideways between dripping columns.
spotlights.story_md: Most visitors meet Meghalaya's caves at **Mawsmai**, a short lit cave a few kilometres from Sohra, where the route narrows to body width between stalactites. Nearby **Arwah** cave has fossils of shells and fish set in its walls, a reminder that this rock formed under a sea. These are small. The real caving is far out in the Jaintia and Garo hills, mapped since 1992 by Meghalayan and European cavers in a long project called Caving in the Abode of the Clouds. They have surveyed hundreds of kilometres of passage.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The caves turn a rainy plateau into a world-class destination for cavers.
spotlights.memory_hook: Squeeze sideways through Mawsmai, then imagine 34 km more of it.

spotlights.name: Krem Liat Prah
spotlights.spot_it: No sign, no lights: a hole in the forest floor on a ridge pitted with about 150 caves.
spotlights.story_md: **Krem Liat Prah** ('krem' means cave in Khasi) is the longest known natural cave in South Asia, at about **34 km** of surveyed passage, and expeditions keep adding to it. It lies under the Shnongrim ridge in East Jaintia Hills, an area with about 150 known caves. Nearby **Synrang Pamiang** is the deepest in the state. Cavers have found blind fish and other animals adapted to total darkness. The same hills are also the heart of coal mining, and caving teams have warned that mining and limestone quarrying threaten passages that have not even been mapped yet.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It puts Meghalaya on the world caving map.
spotlights.memory_hook: 34 km of darkness under one ridge, and the map is still growing.

spotlights.name: Mawmluh cave and the Meghalayan Age
spotlights.spot_it: A dark cave mouth near Sohra whose name is now printed on the geological time scale.
spotlights.story_md: In June 2018 geologists officially split the Holocene, the last 11,700 years, into three ages. The youngest, from **4,200 years ago** to today, is called the **Meghalayan**. Its start is fixed by a stalagmite from **Krem Mawmluh**, a 7.2 km cave near Sohra. Layers in that stalagmite record a sharp drop in monsoon rain at about 4,200 years ago, part of a global megadrought that hit Egypt, Mesopotamia, the Indus cities and China. In 2022 the IUGS listed the Mawmluh site among its first 100 geological heritage sites.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Everyone alive today lives in an age named after Meghalaya.
spotlights.memory_hook: You are living in the Meghalayan: a stalagmite from Sohra says so.

spotlights.name: Laitlum canyons
spotlights.spot_it: A grassy ridge ending in sudden drops into canyons, with a village far below.
spotlights.story_md: Laitlum, a short drive south-east of Shillong, is where the plateau top ends and the land falls away into steep, forested canyons. From the ridge you can see villages and terraced fields hundreds of metres below, joined to the top by long stone stairways. Locals walk these paths daily, carrying loads on their backs with a strap across the forehead. In the monsoon the canyons fill with cloud in minutes. The name is often glossed as 'end of the hills'.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows the plateau's edge without the crowds of Sohra.
spotlights.memory_hook: Laitlum: where the hills end and the stairs begin.

spotlights.name: Umiam Lake
spotlights.spot_it: A big blue reservoir with fingers of water between pine hills, 15 km north of Shillong.
spotlights.story_md: Most first-time visitors think Umiam is a natural lake. It is a reservoir, created when the Umiam river was dammed in the early 1960s by the Assam State Electricity Board. Its first powerhouse, four 9 MW turbines, began commercial operation in 1965, the first reservoir hydro project in north-east India. Locals still call the area **Barapani**, 'big water'. Today the lake is used for kayaking and sailing, and it is also silting up as hills around it are cleared.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the first sight of Meghalaya for anyone driving up from Guwahati.
spotlights.memory_hook: Barapani: the 'lake' that is really a 1960s power plant.

sections.title: Forests, apes and a plant that eats insects
sections.intro_md:
Rain and steep ground have kept much of Meghalaya forested: official estimates put tree and forest cover at around three quarters of the land, though most of it is community land, not government reserve. That is the key fact about nature here. Under the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution, about 90% of forests belong to clans, villages and district councils, not the state forest department.

The forests sit where the Indian, Malayan and Chinese worlds of plants and animals overlap. Meghalaya has India's only ape, the **hoolock gibbon**, clouded leopards, hundreds of bird species, and the only pitcher plant native to India. Wild orange trees grow on Nokrek. Some of the best-kept forest survives because it is **sacred**: groves where taking even a dead leaf is forbidden.

The threats are the familiar ones, plus some local ones: shifting cultivation on shorter cycles, coal and limestone mining, roads, and towns spreading along ridges.

spotlights.name: Western hoolock gibbon

where.label: Garo Hills and Khasi Hills forests

spotlights.spot_it: A tailless ape swinging arm over arm through the canopy; black males with white brows, blond females.
spotlights.story_md: The hoolock is the only ape found in India, and Meghalaya's Garo Hills are among its strongholds. Adults pair for life and sing duets at dawn, whooping calls that carry more than a kilometre through the forest. Males are black with a white brow; females are buff or golden, so a pair looks like two different species. Gibbons almost never come to the ground, which makes them helpless when forest is broken up by roads and jhum clearings. The species is listed as Endangered.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's only ape depends on unbroken canopy, and Meghalaya still has some.
spotlights.memory_hook: Black husband, blond wife, and a duet every sunrise.

spotlights.name: The Khasi pitcher plant
spotlights.spot_it: Green-and-red cups with a lid, hanging off the tips of leaves in wet scrub.
spotlights.story_md: **Nepenthes khasiana** is the only pitcher plant native to India and grows almost nowhere outside Meghalaya's hills. Each pitcher is a modified leaf tip. Insects are drawn by nectar and colour, slip on a waxy rim and drown in digestive fluid at the bottom; the plant takes nitrogen from them, which the leached, rain-washed soil cannot give it. In Khasi it is sometimes called **tiew-rakot**, the demon flower. Collection for gardens and loss of habitat pushed it to Endangered.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a plant adapted to exactly the poor soil that so much rain creates.
spotlights.memory_hook: In soil washed bare by rain, the plant learned to eat flies.

spotlights.name: Mawphlang sacred forest
spotlights.spot_it: A sudden island of tall, moss-hung forest in open grassland, with standing stones inside.
spotlights.story_md: The **law kyntang**, sacred forest, at Mawphlang is about 25 km from Shillong. Khasi belief holds it is home to a guardian spirit, recorded as **U Basa** or U Ryngkew, and the rule is simple: nothing leaves the forest. Not a log, not a dead leaf, not a flower. Locals say anyone who breaks the rule falls ill. The result is old-growth forest with huge trees, fungi, orchids and monoliths where rituals were held, a few minutes from treeless hills. Many Khasi villages once kept such a grove, and dozens still do.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Belief protected forest better than law did.
spotlights.memory_hook: Take nothing, not even a leaf: the grove's spirit is watching.

spotlights.name: Nokrek and the mother of oranges
spotlights.spot_it: The highest ridge of the Garo Hills, cloud forest on top, jhum patches on the slopes.
spotlights.story_md: Nokrek peak (1,412 m) is the core of a UNESCO-recognised biosphere reserve. Its forests hold **Citrus indica**, the Indian wild orange, which botanists treat as one of the wild ancestors of cultivated citrus. A gene sanctuary was set up to protect it. Garo villagers call it **memang narang**, the 'orange of the spirits', and used it as medicine. The reserve also has elephants, hoolock gibbons and red pandas have been reported. Around it, villages practise **jhum**, cutting and burning a patch of forest, farming it for a year or two, then moving on.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Part of the family tree of your morning orange juice grows wild here.
spotlights.memory_hook: Memang narang: the spirits' orange, grandmother of the ones in shops.

sections.title: Bridges that grow
sections.intro_md:
In the gorges below Sohra the rivers flood so hard in the monsoon that wooden bridges rot or wash away within a few years. The War Khasi and other villagers found an answer in the **rubber fig**, *Ficus elastica*, which throws out aerial roots that grow toward the ground and thicken when they touch it.

Villagers train those roots across a stream, sometimes along bamboo or hollowed areca palm trunks, and wait. It can take **15 years or more** before a bridge carries a person. After that it gets stronger every year. Researchers led by Ferdinand Ludwig of the Technical University of Munich have geo-located about **75** living bridges, and estimate some are centuries old. The longest known, near Rangthylliang, spans more than **50 m**.

In 2022 India put the root bridge landscapes of the Khasi and Jaintia hills, called **Jingkieng Jri**, on its tentative list for UNESCO World Heritage status.

data.label: First written record
data.note: Henry Yule, Asiatic Society of Bengal

spotlights.name: The double decker root bridge, Nongriat
spotlights.spot_it: Two root bridges stacked one above the other over a blue pool, reached by about 3,500 steps.
spotlights.story_md: From the village of Tyrna, a stairway of roughly 3,500 concrete steps drops through forest to **Nongriat**, a village of a few dozen households. Next to it is the most famous root bridge in the world: two decks of living roots, one above the other, across the Umshiang stream. Locals say the second deck was grown because the river rose too high in the monsoon. It is estimated to be around 200 years old. Nongriat villagers have since begun a third level. The walk back up is the part visitors remember.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the image that made root bridges globally famous.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two floors of living tree, and 3,500 steps to get home.

spotlights.name: How a root bridge is grown
spotlights.when: Practised for at least two centuries
spotlights.spot_it: A walkway of interlaced roots, often with stones pressed into the gaps, and rails of roots at hand height.
spotlights.story_md: A rubber fig is planted or found on the bank. Its aerial roots are guided across the stream, along bamboo scaffolding or through split areca trunks. As roots touch each other they fuse, a process botanists call **inosculation**, and form a living mesh. Builders tie in more roots each season and lay stones in the deck. Mature bridges can hold dozens of people at once. The first written description in English came from the Scottish officer **Henry Yule**, who published a drawing in the Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal in **1844**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is engineering on a timescale of generations: you plant a bridge for your grandchildren.
spotlights.memory_hook: Plant it, guide it, wait 15 years, then walk across a tree.

sections.title: Three hill peoples, two language families
sections.intro_md:
Meghalaya's map is often drawn as three blocks, named after the people who live there: the **Garo Hills** in the west, the **Khasi Hills** in the centre and the **Jaintia Hills** in the east.

The **Khasi** and **Pnar** (Jaintia) speak Khasian languages of the **Austroasiatic** family, related to Mon and Khmer in South-East Asia and to Munda languages like Santali. The Khasi call themselves **Ki Hynñiewtrep**, the children of the seven huts, after a myth in which sixteen families once moved freely between earth and heaven by a ladder on Sohpetbneng peak, until seven were cut off on earth. The **Garo**, or A·chik, speak a **Tibeto-Burman** language related to Bodo and Tripuri, and trace their origin to a migration from Tibet.

The 2011 census found Khasi spoken by 33.8% of people, Garo by 31.6%, Pnar by 10.7% and Bengali by 6.4%. Smaller groups include the Hajong, Koch, Rabha, Biate and War. Hindi speakers are under 2%.

spotlights.name: The Khasi
spotlights.spot_it: Women in a jainsem, a pinafore-like silk tied at the shoulders; men in a sleeveless jacket and turban.
spotlights.story_md: The Khasi are the largest group in Meghalaya, about 14 lakh people in India in 2011, with smaller communities across the border in Sylhet, Bangladesh. Clans are exogamous: you may not marry inside your clan, which in practice means your mother's surname. Traditional government ran through about 25 small states called **hima**, each under a **syiem** chosen from a royal clan and checked by a council. Village affairs are still run by a **dorbar shnong** and its headman, the **rangbah shnong**. Most Khasi are now Christian, but about 15% followed the indigenous **Niam Khasi** in 2011.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The Khasi kept a matrilineal, self-governing society alive into the 21st century.
spotlights.memory_hook: Seven huts, a ladder to heaven, and your mother's name for life.

spotlights.name: The Garo (A·chik)
spotlights.spot_it: Red, black and white woven dakmanda wraps, beaded necklaces and feather-topped headgear at festivals.
spotlights.story_md: The Garo call themselves **A·chik Mande**, 'hill people'. Their oral history says they came from Tibet around 400 BCE under leaders named Jappa Jalimpa, Sukpa and Bongepa, and crossed the Brahmaputra into these hills. Children take their mother's clan title. A husband traditionally moves into his wife's home. Villages kept a **nokpante**, a bachelors' dormitory where young men were trained and women were not allowed. About 90% are now Christian, while the traditional faith, **Songsarek**, survives in some villages. The 1872 British expedition into the Garo Hills met warriors armed with swords and shields against rifles.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The Garo are the second matrilineal people of the state, with their own language, faith and festivals.
spotlights.memory_hook: A·chik Mande: hill people who say they walked here from Tibet.

spotlights.name: The Pnar (Jaintia)
spotlights.spot_it: The crowds at Jowai's Behdienkhlam: the Pnar festival that the whole state comes to watch.
spotlights.story_md: The Pnar are the people of the Jaintia Hills, centred on **Jowai**. Their language is close to Khasi, and many count them as part of the wider Hynñiewtrep family, but they ruled their own kingdom, the **Jaintia** state, which stretched from the hills down into the plains of Sylhet. Pnar society is also matrilineal. A larger share of Pnar than of Khasi still follow the indigenous faith, called **Niamtre** in the Jaintia Hills, which is why the big seasonal festivals there remain so strong. The Pnar country is also the coal and limestone belt, which has made it the richest and most scarred part of the state.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The Pnar had a kingdom with a plains capital long before there was a Meghalaya.
spotlights.memory_hook: Same family as the Khasi, but they had a king and a capital in Bangladesh.

sections.title: Where the youngest daughter inherits
sections.intro_md:
Meghalaya is the largest matrilineal society in India and one of the largest anywhere. Among the Khasi, Pnar and Garo, children take their **mother's clan name**, and family property passes down the female line.

Matrilineal does not mean matriarchal. Women own and inherit, but traditional political power sat with men: the syiem, the village headman and the dorbar were male, and in many villages women still cannot sit on the dorbar. The maternal uncle, the **kñi**, traditionally handled clan decisions.

The system is debated inside the state. Some Khasi men's groups have campaigned since the 1990s to shift to the father's line. A 2023 Khasi Hills council proposal to deny tribal status to Khasi who take their father's surname caused an uproar. Women's rights writers, such as the Shillong editor **Patricia Mukhim**, point out that inheriting the family house can also mean inheriting the duty to care for everyone in it. In the 2023 elections only three women won seats in the 60-member assembly.

spotlights.name: Ka khadduh, the youngest daughter
spotlights.spot_it: The ancestral house, the hearth and the family's ritual duties stay with the youngest daughter.
spotlights.story_md: In a Khasi family the youngest daughter, **ka khadduh**, inherits the ancestral house and most of the family property. She does not own it in the Western sense: she is its keeper. She must look after her parents in old age, care for unmarried or returning siblings, and perform the clan's rites. When she marries, her husband traditionally moves in with her family. If a family has no daughter, it may adopt a girl to continue the line. Older sisters often get a share and set up their own homes nearby.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It flips the usual Indian pattern of sons inheriting and daughters leaving.
spotlights.memory_hook: The last-born daughter holds the house keys, and the duty that comes with them.

spotlights.name: The Garo house and the nokpante
spotlights.spot_it: A long house of bamboo and thatch raised on stilts, its front room open for guests.
spotlights.story_md: A Garo daughter chosen as heiress, the **nokna**, inherits the house, and her husband, often a cousin from her father's clan, joins her household. The village **nokma** (headman) traditionally held office through his wife's line. Young unmarried men slept in the **nokpante**, a carved bachelors' house near the village centre that was also school, guard post and guesthouse. The nokpante faded as missions and schools spread, but Garo villages still build long houses on stilts that keep floors dry in the rain and animals underneath.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows a second, distinct form of matriliny, not a copy of the Khasi one.
spotlights.memory_hook: The heiress keeps the house; the bachelors sleep in the nokpante.

spotlights.name: Iewduh, the women's market
spotlights.when: One of the oldest markets in the region
spotlights.spot_it: A maze of stalls where almost every seller of fish, pork, betel and cloth is a woman.
spotlights.story_md: **Iewduh**, which outsiders call Bara Bazar, is Shillong's old market, a warren of lanes running down a hillside. Its traders are overwhelmingly women, many of them running businesses passed from mother to daughter. The market follows the traditional Khasi eight-day week, and was historically under the authority of the Syiem of Mylliem rather than the city. Walk through and you see matriliny as economics: women controlling stock, cash and credit. It is also the best place to buy kwai, tungrymbai and fresh silkworms.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is where women's economic power is most visible.
spotlights.memory_hook: Iewduh: eight-day weeks and a woman behind every till.

sections.title: Stones, kingdoms and a war over a road
sections.intro_md:
Meghalaya's deep history is written in stone rather than on paper. Across the hills stand thousands of **monoliths**: upright stones, **menhirs**, raised for male ancestors, and flat table stones, **dolmens**, for female ones, often in rows beside old paths and markets. Stone tools show people here for tens of thousands of years, but the Khasi had no script of their own, so the written record begins with neighbours and colonists.

By the 16th century the Khasi lived in about 25 small states, the **hima**, while the Pnar formed the **Jaintia kingdom**, with a winter capital at Jaintiapur in the plains and a summer seat at **Nartiang**. The Garo lived in independent villages.

The British arrived after 1824, when they took Assam from Burma. They wanted a road from the Brahmaputra valley to Sylhet across the hills. That road started the **Anglo-Khasi War** in 1829. The Jaintia kingdom was annexed in 1835, the Garo Hills brought under control in 1872 and 1873, and Shillong became a colonial capital in 1874.

spotlights.name: The Khasi monoliths

where.label: Across the Khasi Hills; many near Sohra and Mawphlang

spotlights.when: Raised over many centuries; some still raised in the 20th century
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of tall rough slabs, with flat stone tables laid in front of them.
spotlights.story_md: Khasi monoliths come in pairs of ideas. The upright stones, **mawbynna**, honour male ancestors, usually the maternal uncles of the clan. The flat table stone in front, **mawkynthei**, honours the female line, the clan mother. They were raised after a family moved the bones of its dead into a common clan ossuary, and some served as rest stops on market paths, where travellers sat on the table stones. Raising one could take hundreds of people pulling stone on wooden rollers.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They are the archive of a society that wrote nothing down.
spotlights.memory_hook: Standing stones for the uncles, a stone table for the mother.

spotlights.name: Nartiang monoliths
spotlights.when: Associated with the Jaintia kings, 16th to 18th centuries
spotlights.spot_it: A garden of grey slabs, dozens of them, some taller than a two-storey house.
spotlights.story_md: Nartiang, 65 km from Shillong, was the summer seat of the Jaintia kings. Its monolith garden is one of the largest collections of standing stones in the region, and tradition says the tallest, about 8 m, was raised by a giant named **U Mar Phalyngki** who carried it from a nearby quarry. Close by is the **Nartiang Durga temple**, said to be about 600 years old and counted by devotees as one of the Shakti pithas. It is a reminder that Jaintia kings combined Hindu and indigenous rites. British accounts of human sacrifice at shrines in the kingdom were used to justify annexing it in 1835.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows a hill kingdom that blended Hindu and Khasi-Pnar traditions.
spotlights.memory_hook: Stones carried by a giant, beside a goddess's temple.

spotlights.name: U Tirot Sing
spotlights.spot_it: The syiem whose statue stands at Mairang, and whose death day is a state holiday.
spotlights.story_md: Tirot Sing was the **Syiem of Nongkhlaw**, a small Khasi state on the British road route. He first agreed to let David Scott, the British agent, build the Guwahati to Sylhet road through his land, hoping to win back trade passes on the Assam plains. When the British reinforced their posts instead, he ordered them out. On **4 April 1829** Khasi fighters attacked the British at Nongkhlaw. The war lasted about four years, fought with swords, bows and ambushes against muskets. In January 1833 he was betrayed for gold, captured and sent to Dhaka, where he died on **17 July 1835**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is Meghalaya's first and best-known anti-colonial hero.
spotlights.memory_hook: He signed for a road, then fought four years to stop it.

spotlights.name: U Kiang Nangbah and Pa Togan Sangma
spotlights.spot_it: Two names on Meghalaya's martyrs' list: a Pnar rebel hanged in Jowai and a Garo warrior who died in battle.
spotlights.story_md: In the Jaintia Hills, British taxes and interference with Pnar rites led to risings in the 1860s. Their leader, **U Kiang Nangbah**, was captured and **hanged in public at Jowai on 30 December 1862**. India issued a stamp for him in 2001. Ten years later, when a British expedition moved into the Garo Hills, **Pa Togan Nengminza Sangma** led Garo warriors in a night attack at Chisobibra. Legend says he gave his men shields of plantain stems, thinking bullets would cool in the wet pith. He was killed on the spot. Both are remembered with statues and state holidays.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Each of Meghalaya's three peoples has a hero of resistance.
spotlights.memory_hook: A hanging in Jowai, and plantain shields against rifles.

spotlights.name: The Great Assam earthquake of 1897
spotlights.spot_it: No ruins remain to see; look instead at Shillong's light wooden 'Assam-type' houses built after it.
spotlights.story_md: At 5 pm on 12 June 1897 a fault along the northern edge of the Shillong Plateau slipped by at least 11 m, one of the largest displacements ever measured. The magnitude is estimated at 8.2 to 8.3. In Shillong every stone house and half the wooden ones were damaged. Around 1,500 people died across the region. The disaster reshaped building: Shillong rebuilt in timber frames with wattle-and-plaster walls and tin roofs, the 'Assam-type' house, which flexes instead of falling. Geologists still study the quake to understand Himalayan risks.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It explains why old Shillong looks the way it does.
spotlights.memory_hook: The plateau jumped 11 m, and Shillong learned to build in wood.

spotlights.name: The 25 Khasi states
spotlights.spot_it: A patchwork map of small chiefdoms, each with its syiem, around British Shillong.
spotlights.story_md: The British never formally annexed most of the Khasi hima. They signed treaties with about **25 Khasi states**, which remained semi-independent, a little like the princely states. Shillong itself sat on land leased from the Syiem of Mylliem. In 1947 the syiems signed an Instrument of Accession and a standstill agreement with India in a special form, and in 1950 the states were folded into the Khasi Hills district under the new Constitution. The syiems survive today as traditional chiefs inside the Khasi Hills Autonomous District Council.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is why traditional institutions still matter so much in Meghalaya politics.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twenty-five tiny kingdoms joined India in 1947, and their chiefs are still there.

sections.title: How Meghalaya became a state, without a war
sections.intro_md:
After 1947 the Khasi, Jaintia and Garo hills were districts of Assam with some self-rule under the **Sixth Schedule**, which created autonomous district councils with powers over land, forests and custom. In 1960 Assam made **Assamese** its sole official language. To hill people who did not speak it, that looked like a door closing.

Hill leaders formed the **All Party Hill Leaders Conference** (APHLC) in 1960 and demanded a separate hill state. They used elections, boycotts and negotiation, not guns, which is unusual in the north-east. In 1969 Parliament passed the Assam Reorganisation (Meghalaya) Act, creating an autonomous state inside Assam from **2 April 1970**. Full statehood came on **21 January 1972**, the same day as Manipur and Tripura. The APHLC's **Williamson A. Sangma**, a Garo, became the first chief minister.

The new state inherited a long, loosely drawn border with Assam. Twelve stretches were disputed. Six were settled in a 2022 agreement, and the rest are still under talks.

spotlights.name: Captain Williamson A. Sangma
spotlights.spot_it: The first chief minister, a Garo leader who had led the hill-state campaign since the 1950s.
spotlights.story_md: Williamson Ampang Sangma began as the first chief executive of the **Garo Hills district council**. In October 1954 he called a conference at Tura of all the hill districts of Assam to demand a hill state, years before the language law turned the demand into a movement. He led the APHLC through the 1960s, and in 1972 was sworn in as the first chief minister of the new state. He later served as Governor of Mizoram. His career shows how the hill-state idea started in the Garo Hills, not only in Shillong.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He turned a district council demand into a new state.
spotlights.memory_hook: From a Tura conference in 1954 to chief minister in 1972.

spotlights.name: P. A. Sangma
spotlights.spot_it: The Garo politician remembered nationally for his cheerful 'Order, order' as Lok Sabha Speaker.
spotlights.story_md: Purno Agitok Sangma was born at Chapahati in the Garo Hills, served as chief minister of Meghalaya from 1988 to 1990, and became the **11th Speaker of the Lok Sabha** from 1996 to 1998, the first from the north-east. He co-founded the Nationalist Congress Party in 1999 and launched the **National People's Party** in 2013, which now governs Meghalaya under his son. In 2012 he ran for President of India and lost to Pranab Mukherjee. He received the Padma Vibhushan posthumously in 2017, the first person from Meghalaya to do so.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He made a small state visible at the very top of Indian politics.
spotlights.memory_hook: From a Garo village to the Speaker's chair, then a party for his son.

spotlights.name: The Assam border dispute
spotlights.when: Six of twelve areas settled in 2022
spotlights.spot_it: Villages where one house pays tax to Shillong and the next to Dispur, and pond ownership becomes a court case.
spotlights.story_md: When Meghalaya was carved out, its line with Assam followed old district boundaries that villagers had never paid much attention to. Twelve stretches came into dispute. On **29 March 2022** the two chief ministers signed an agreement in Delhi settling six of them, splitting about 36.8 km² roughly equally. Tension remained: in November 2022 firing at Mukroh, on the West Jaintia Hills border, during an anti-timber-smuggling operation by Assam forces, killed six people. Talks on the remaining six areas continued into 2025 and 2026.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that statehood created lines on the map that still cost lives.
spotlights.memory_hook: Half the disputes solved on paper, the other half still on the ground.

sections.title: A Welsh alphabet, a whistled name and the old faith
sections.intro_md:
Khasi had no script until Christian missionaries gave it one. Early attempts used the Bengali script, but in **1841** a Welsh Calvinistic Methodist, **Thomas Jones**, arrived in Sohra and wrote Khasi in the **Roman alphabet**, with spelling borrowed partly from Welsh. That is why Khasi is written in Latin letters today, and why the Welsh link is still celebrated in Shillong. Garo, too, is written in Roman script, introduced by American Baptists in the Garo Hills.

The missions brought schools with the Bible, and Meghalaya became one of India's most Christian states: **74.6%** in 2011, split mainly between Presbyterians, Catholics and Baptists. But the old faiths remain. **Niam Khasi** worships a creator, U Blei Nongthaw, and holds that a person should earn righteousness, **kamai ia ka hok**. It was revived from 1899 by the **Seng Khasi** movement, which runs the great spring dance in Shillong. The Garo faith, **Songsarek**, survives in some villages.

In **2026** the state made **Khasi and Garo** full official languages alongside English.

spotlights.name: Thomas Jones, father of the Khasi alphabet
spotlights.spot_it: His grave in Kolkata calls him 'the founding father of the Khasi alphabet and literature'.
spotlights.story_md: Thomas Jones was a carpenter's son from Berriew in mid-Wales. He reached Sohra on **22 June 1841**, learned Khasi, wrote it in Roman letters and produced a **Khasi Reader in 1842**, the first books in the language. He also taught carpentry and new farming methods. He clashed with his own mission and with a British businessman, Harry Inglis, whose treatment of Khasi workers he criticised, and was forced out. He died of malaria in Calcutta in 1849, aged 39. The church at Nongsawlia near Sohra grew from the mission he started.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Every Khasi book, sign and SMS today uses the alphabet he chose.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Welsh carpenter's son gave the Khasi their ABC.

spotlights.name: Kongthong, the whistling village
spotlights.spot_it: Calls echo across the valley that are neither words nor birds: each one is a person's name.
spotlights.story_md: In Kongthong, about 65 km from Shillong, every child gets a second name from its mother: a tune. This **jingrwai iawbei**, roughly 'the melody of the root ancestress', is used to call that person across the hills. Each tune has a long version for calling over a distance and a short one for use at home. Around 700 people share the practice, and nearby villages have similar traditions. When a person dies, their tune dies with them. In 2021 Kongthong was one of India's three nominations for the UN World Tourism Organization's Best Tourism Villages.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the world's rare whistled naming systems.
spotlights.memory_hook: In Kongthong your mother hums your name, and it is never used again.

spotlights.name: Niam Khasi and the Seng Khasi
spotlights.spot_it: No temples and no idols: rites at stones, in sacred groves and at the family hearth.
spotlights.story_md: The indigenous Khasi faith has no scripture and no images. Its creator, **U Blei Nongthaw**, is approached through clan rites, offerings at monoliths and in groves, and reading the future in eggs and entrails. Its moral core is three sayings: know man and God, know your father's and mother's kin, and earn righteousness. In 1899, worried that Christianity would sweep away the old ways, sixteen young Khasi men founded the **Seng Khasi** to protect them. The Seng still organises Shad Suk Mynsiem. In the Garo Hills the matching faith is **Songsarek**, centred on the god Saljong and harvest rites.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It explains why Christian Meghalaya still has living indigenous festivals.
spotlights.memory_hook: Earn your righteousness: no book, no idol, just stones and kin.

sections.title: Dance as worship: the festival year
sections.intro_md:
In Meghalaya the big festivals are danced. Khasi tradition holds that dance is a form of thanksgiving, so the great rites are performed rather than watched: rows of dancers moving for hours in silk, gold and silver.

The year runs roughly like this. In **April** the Seng Khasi hold **Shad Suk Mynsiem**, the dance of the joyful heart, in Shillong. In **July**, after sowing, the Pnar of Jowai drive out disease at **Behdienkhlam**. In **autumn** the Garo give thanks for the harvest at **Wangala**, ending in the **100 Drums** festival near Tura in November. Also in autumn, the old Khyrim state holds the **Nongkrem dance** at Smit. And in **December** the whole state lights up for **Christmas**, which in Shillong means carols, lights strung across Police Bazar and midnight services in packed churches.

None of these is staged for tourists, but all welcome them. The rule of thumb: ask before photographing rites, and do not step into the dance ground.

data.name: Behdienkhlam, Jowai; U Tirot Sing Day, 17 July

spotlights.name: Shad Suk Mynsiem
spotlights.spot_it: Women in an inner circle, eyes lowered, shuffling slowly; men in an outer ring, leaping with swords and whisks.
spotlights.story_md: The 'dance of the joyful heart' is a spring thanksgiving held over three days by the Seng Khasi. Unmarried women dance in the centre, wearing silk and gold crowns, moving with tiny steps and downcast eyes. The men circle them, holding a sword in the right hand and a yak-hair whisk in the left, and move faster. Read it as a picture of Khasi society: the woman is the centre, the keeper of the clan; the man is the protector on the outside. Drums and the tangmuri, a reed pipe, set the rhythm.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most visible statement of Khasi identity each year.
spotlights.memory_hook: Women in the middle, eyes down; men outside with swords.

spotlights.name: Nongkrem dance at Smit
spotlights.spot_it: Dancers before the syiem's house at Smit, with goats offered for the harvest.
spotlights.story_md: Smit, 11 km from Shillong, is the seat of the **Syiem of Hima Khyrim**. Each autumn it holds the Nongkrem dance, a five-day rite of thanksgiving to the goddess **Ka Blei Synshar** for the harvest and prayer for the next one. The syiem and the high priestess, the **syiem sad**, who is the syiem's sister or another woman of the royal line, perform rites at the royal house, and goats are sacrificed. Then young women in silk and young men with swords dance in front of the house. The ritual role of the priestess is a living example of the clan mother's power.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the few surviving royal rites of a Khasi state.
spotlights.memory_hook: A syiem, his priestess sister and a dance for the harvest goddess.

spotlights.name: Behdienkhlam
spotlights.spot_it: Men wrestling a huge log in a pool of mud while drums thunder and the crowd roars.
spotlights.story_md: The name comes from Pnar words for 'to drive away' and 'disease'; the festival was held to chase out the cholera demon. Over several days in Jowai, men beat the roofs of every house with bamboo to drive spirits out. Tall decorated towers are carried through town. On the last day, polished logs are plunged into **Aitnar**, a muddy pool, and men of different localities fight over a great log in a tussle called **Iatan-Bhang**. A football-like game with a wooden ball follows, and its result is read as a forecast of the harvest. Women do not dance; they prepare food and offerings.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the biggest festival of the Pnar faith, held in a mostly Christian state.
spotlights.memory_hook: Beat the roofs, drown the logs, wrestle the mud: cholera, be gone.

spotlights.name: Wangala and the 100 Drums
spotlights.spot_it: Two long lines of dancers, men beating long oval drums, women in red, all moving in slow steps.
spotlights.story_md: Wangala is the Garo thanksgiving to **Misi Saljong**, the provider of harvests, held after the crops are in. In each village a priest, the **kamal**, pours rice beer in the nokma's house in a rite called rugala and burns incense. Then the dance, **dama gogata**: men beating the long dama drums and blowing buffalo-horn trumpets, women dancing in lines. Since **December 1976** a state-supported '100 Drums Wangala' has been held at Asanang, 18 km from Tura, where troupes from across the Garo Hills compete with a hundred drums sounding at once.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the Garo identity festival, and a spectacle of sound.
spotlights.memory_hook: A hundred drums for the god who sends the rice.

spotlights.name: Christmas in Shillong
spotlights.spot_it: Street-wide arches of lights, stars on every house and carol groups at midnight.
spotlights.story_md: With three quarters of the state Christian, December is the main holiday season. Shillong strings lights across its streets, houses hang paper stars, and church choirs go from house to house singing carols in Khasi and English. Many families attend midnight service, then eat late into the night. The city has a strong choral tradition, and some of its choirs now tour the world. Christmas also overlaps with Shillong's winter music season and the New Year, so hotels fill with visitors from the rest of India.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how Christianity has become part of local culture, not just a faith.
spotlights.memory_hook: Carols in Khasi and stars on every roof.

sections.title: India's rock capital and its choir
sections.intro_md:
Ask anyone in India's music business where the guitarists come from, and Shillong will come up. Christian schools taught Western music and choir singing; radio and records brought Elvis, Dylan and the Beatles in the 1960s; and Khasi homes already sang in harmony. The result is a city where teenagers play the blues in bars, every church has a choir, and an annual concert for Bob Dylan's birthday has been running for more than fifty years.

The traditional side is just as alive: the **duitara**, a plucked lute, the **ksing** drums and the **tangmuri** reed pipe of the Khasi; the **dama** drums and buffalo-horn trumpets of the Garo.

Sport here means two things. **Football** is the passion, with Shillong Lajong FC and players like Eugeneson Lyngdoh reaching the national team. And **archery**, an old Khasi sport, feeds one of India's oddest legal betting games, **teer**, whose results are announced every afternoon except Sundays.

spotlights.name: Lou Majaw
spotlights.spot_it: A white-haired rocker in shorts, whatever the weather, with an acoustic guitar.
spotlights.story_md: Lou Majaw was born in Shillong in 1947 and became the face of its rock scene. In 1972 he organised a concert to mark **Bob Dylan's birthday on 24 May**, and he has held one every year since, making it one of the longest-running tribute shows anywhere. Majaw is famous for performing in shorts. He played in Kolkata's club circuit in the 1960s and 1970s before coming home, and has mentored generations of Shillong musicians. Dylan has never played the show.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He made Shillong's love of rock into a civic tradition.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fifty years of birthday songs for a man who never came.

spotlights.name: The Shillong Chamber Choir
spotlights.spot_it: Voices in tight harmony, singing Khasi hymns, Hindi film songs and opera in one evening.
spotlights.story_md: Founded in 2001 by the composer and pianist **Neil Nongkynrih**, who trained at Trinity College and the Guildhall School in London, the choir won three gold diplomas at the World Choir Games in China in July 2010, then won **India's Got Talent** that October. In November 2010 it sang for Barack and Michelle Obama at Rashtrapati Bhavan. It sings in more than 15 languages and is known for mixing Western classical, Bollywood and Khasi songs. Nongkynrih received the **Padma Shri in 2015**. The choir continues to tour, with Khasi songs he wrote still in its repertoire.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It took Shillong's church singing to a national audience.
spotlights.memory_hook: From Khasi hymns to the Obamas' dinner in one year.

spotlights.name: Soulmate
spotlights.spot_it: A woman with a huge blues voice and a guitarist playing long, slow solos.
spotlights.story_md: Soulmate, formed in Shillong in 2003 by singer **Tipriti Kharbangar** and guitarist **Rudy Wallang**, is often called India's leading blues band. They have played festivals across India and abroad, and their records mix Chicago blues with Khasi themes. The band sums up the Shillong formula: church-trained voices, guitar skills learned from records and radio, and a city of small bars and live venues. Rudy Wallang is also an elder statesman of the local scene, playing since the 1970s.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It proved a hill-town blues band could build a national career.
spotlights.memory_hook: Chicago blues, with Shillong rain on the windows.

spotlights.name: The duitara
spotlights.spot_it: A small, long-necked wooden lute plucked with a bamboo or wooden pick.
spotlights.story_md: The duitara is the classic Khasi string instrument, carved from a single block of wood with a skin-covered body and usually four strings. It is plucked with a small pick and accompanies songs and stories, especially the long sung narratives of Khasi folklore. With the **ksing** drums and the **tangmuri**, a double-reed pipe heard at dances, it makes up the core of traditional Khasi music. Young Shillong musicians now mix the duitara into folk-rock, the way their parents mixed in electric guitars.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the sound of Khasi tradition before the guitar arrived.
spotlights.memory_hook: Four strings and a pick: the guitar's Khasi cousin.

spotlights.name: Teer: betting on arrows
spotlights.spot_it: Dozens of archers in a semicircle loosing arrows at a small drum-shaped target of straw.
spotlights.story_md: Every weekday afternoon in Shillong, members of archery clubs shoot thousands of arrows at a straw target for a few minutes. The arrows that hit are counted, and the **last two digits** of the total are the winning number. People bet on that number at small counters across the state, often after consulting dream books that turn dreams into numbers: a snake might mean one number, a wedding another. A second round follows. The game is legal, licensed and taxed by the state, and results are posted within the hour.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turns an ancient sport into a daily economy, and a daily superstition.
spotlights.memory_hook: Dream of a snake, count the arrows, keep the last two digits.

sections.title: Silk, gold, beads and drums: what people wear and make
sections.intro_md:
Khasi festival dress is some of the most expensive in India, because so much of it is **gold**. A dancer at Shad Suk Mynsiem may wear a crown, heavy gold and coral necklaces, gold wrist ornaments and silver chains, much of it heirloom jewellery kept by the clan. The silk is local too: Meghalaya produces **eri** (Ri-Bhoi's 'peace silk', spun without killing the moth) and **muga**, and its Khasi eri silk received a GI tag in 2024.

Everyday dress for Khasi women is the **jainsem**, two lengths of cloth knotted at the shoulders and worn over a blouse, often with a checked shawl, the **tapmohkhlieh**, against the cold. Garo women wear the **dakmanda**, a woven wrap with bold borders. Men wear the jymphong, a sleeveless coat, for ceremonies.

Craft here is practical: cane and bamboo baskets of every shape, including the conical **khoh** carried on the back with a head strap, mats, umbrellas and fish traps. Most households still make some of their own.

spotlights.name: The jainsem and dhara
spotlights.spot_it: A loose, sleeveless overdress knotted on both shoulders over a blouse and skirt.
spotlights.story_md: The **jainsem** is made of two rectangles of cloth pinned or knotted at the shoulders, falling straight to the calf, with no stitching to shape it. It is worn over a blouse and a wrap skirt. For festivals it becomes the **dhara**, a richer version in mulberry or muga silk, worn with a gold or silver crown. Pnar women wear the related **thoh kyrshah**, a checked cloth. Visitors are often surprised that Khasi women wear the jainsem to offices and markets every day, not just for photographs.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most recognisable piece of Khasi identity.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two cloths, two knots, no seams: the jainsem.

spotlights.name: Ka pansngiat and Khasi gold
spotlights.spot_it: A silver or gold crown with a tall spike at the back, worn by women dancers.
spotlights.story_md: The **pansngiat** is the crown worn by unmarried women at Shad Suk Mynsiem and Nongkrem, a band of silver or gold with a pointed plume rising at the back. It is worn with the **kynjri ksiar**, gold and red coral necklaces, and the **khadu**, a heavy wrist ornament. Men dance with silver quivers and swords. These pieces are clan property, handed down the female line along with the house, and a full set can be worth a small fortune. Some Shillong goldsmiths make nothing else.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that matrilineal inheritance includes portable wealth.
spotlights.memory_hook: A crown with a spike, and gold that belongs to the clan, not the dancer.

spotlights.name: Dakmanda, sengki and Garo ornaments
spotlights.spot_it: A woven wrap with a wide patterned border, a beaded waist band and a tall feathered hair pin.
spotlights.story_md: Garo women's festival dress centres on the **dakmanda**, a handwoven wrap whose border, the **dakmanda**'s decorated panel, shows a weaver's skill. It is worn with a blouse, the **dakshari**. Ornaments include the **sengki**, a waist band once made from ivory or bone beads and now from plastic or glass, and the **pilne**, a hair ornament topped with feathers. Men at Wangala wear feathered turbans. The Garo dakmanda received a GI tag in 2024.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Garo dress is a separate tradition from Khasi dress, and easy to tell apart.
spotlights.memory_hook: Red and black borders, a bead belt and a feather pin: that is Garo.

sections.title: Pork, fermented beans and a betel nut on arrival
sections.intro_md:
Meghalaya cooks with little oil and less spice than the plains, but a lot of **pork**, **fermented** flavours, **black sesame** and fresh herbs. Rice is the base of every meal; the state grows dozens of local varieties, including sticky and red rice.

The Khasi table has **jadoh**, rice cooked with pork and its fat, **doh khlieh**, a pork salad with onion and ginger, **dohneiiong**, pork in a black sesame gravy, and **tungrymbai**, fermented soybean. The Garo kitchen is built on dried fish, bamboo shoot and **kapa**, cooked with an alkaline ash water, **kalchi**, instead of oil: **nakham bitchi**, a dried fish soup, is the classic. Everyone drinks local rice beer at rites, and tea everywhere else.

At the edges of the plate sit the state's famous crops: Khasi mandarins, pineapples from Ri-Bhoi and the Garo hills, and the bright orange **Lakadong turmeric**. And before or after any visit comes **kwai**.

spotlights.name: Jadoh
spotlights.spot_it: Reddish-yellow rice glistening with pork fat, served in roadside 'jadoh stalls'.
spotlights.story_md: Jadoh is rice cooked with pieces of pork, its fat and its blood or offal, often coloured yellow with local turmeric and flavoured with ginger, onion and bay leaf. It is the Khasi breakfast-lunch-anytime meal, served in small eateries with sides of fried pork, fermented soybean chutney and chilli. Variations use chicken or fish. Families serve it at gatherings in big pots. To outsiders it looks like a pulao; the taste is closer to a rich, meaty congee.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the one dish that says 'Khasi kitchen'.
spotlights.memory_hook: Rice that has met a pig: jadoh.

spotlights.name: Tungrymbai
spotlights.spot_it: Brownish fermented soybeans with a strong smell, cooked into a thick black-sesame paste with pork.
spotlights.story_md: To make tungrymbai, soybeans are boiled, drained and packed into a bamboo basket lined with fresh **slamet** leaves (*Phrynium pubinerve*). Hot charcoal goes on top, the basket is wrapped in a jute bag and left by the fireplace for three to four days. The fermented beans are pounded in a wooden mortar and fried in mustard oil with onion, ginger, garlic, black sesame paste and pork. It is a relative of Japanese natto and Naga axone: north-east India and East Asia share a fermented-bean belt.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows Meghalaya's links to the food cultures of East Asia.
spotlights.memory_hook: Beans, leaves, charcoal, three days: tungrymbai.

spotlights.name: Kwai, the betel welcome
spotlights.spot_it: Red-stained lips and a small leaf parcel offered to every visitor.
spotlights.story_md: **Kwai** is raw areca nut, betel leaf and a smear of lime, chewed together until the mouth turns red. Offering it is the basic Khasi act of hospitality: a guest is given kwai before anything else, and refusing it can seem rude. It turns up in rites, weddings and even in the Nohkalikai legend, where Likai finds her child's finger in the kwai basket. A Khasi saying holds that God gave kwai to humans to share. Areca nut is also a major cash crop, and a known cause of oral cancer.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the social glue of daily life in the hills.
spotlights.memory_hook: Before you sit down, you are handed kwai.

spotlights.name: Lakadong turmeric
spotlights.spot_it: Turmeric of an unusually deep orange colour, sold as dried chips and powder.
spotlights.story_md: Turmeric from the Lakadong area of the Jaintia Hills is among the richest in the world in **curcumin**, the compound that gives turmeric its colour: about **6.8 to 7.5%**, against roughly 2 to 3% in ordinary varieties. The state backed it with a 'Mission Lakadong' programme, and it received a Geographical Indication tag on **30 March 2024**. Much of the push came from a teacher in Mulieh village, **Trinity Saioo**, who organised women farmers into self-help groups and was given the **Padma Shri in 2020**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A small hill crop competes on quality, not volume.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twice the curcumin, thanks partly to a village schoolteacher.

sections.title: Places to go
sections.intro_md:
Most visitors fly or drive to Shillong from Guwahati, about 100 km and three hours away, and make day trips south to Sohra and Mawlynnong. That route covers the classics: the living root bridges, Nohkalikai, the caves, Dawki's clear river and the plateau's edge. The best months are **October to April**, when roads are dry and the river runs clear. The monsoon, **June to September**, is when the waterfalls are at full force and the clouds roll through the valleys, but landslides close roads.

The less visited half of the state is the west. The **Garo Hills** around Tura have Nokrek, Balpakram's canyon and the bat cave at Siju, and get a fraction of Shillong's visitors. In the east, the **Jaintia Hills** have Krang Suri falls, Nartiang and the caves of Shnongrim.

A note on behaviour: many villages charge a small entry or parking fee that funds cleaning, and some sacred sites restrict photographs.

spotlights.name: Mawlynnong
spotlights.spot_it: Swept paths, flower beds, and bamboo dustbins at every few steps.
spotlights.story_md: In 2003 the travel magazine *Discover India* named this border village of about 95 households 'the cleanest village in Asia', and it became famous overnight. The cleanliness is old custom: every resident joins village clean-ups, plastic bags and smoking are banned, rubbish goes into conical **bamboo bins** and is composted in pits. Tourism raised incomes by around 60% by one 2017 report, though some villagers say the crowds have strained the place. Nearby are a root bridge at Riwai and a boulder balanced on a small stone.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows community rules achieving what municipal budgets often cannot.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bamboo bins on every corner, and a prize from 2003 that never wore off.

spotlights.name: Krang Suri falls
spotlights.spot_it: A wide curtain of water falling into a turquoise pool, with a cave behind the fall.
spotlights.story_md: Krang Suri lies in the Jaintia Hills, about 80 km from Shillong. Its water drops into a clear, deep pool coloured blue by limestone, and a walkway lets visitors go behind the curtain of water to a small cave. Swimming is allowed with life jackets in the dry season. It is managed by the local community, which charges an entry fee and keeps the site tidy, a pattern repeated across many Meghalaya beauty spots.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows the Jaintia Hills have attractions to rival Sohra's.
spotlights.memory_hook: Walk behind the water into the cave.

spotlights.name: Siju cave
spotlights.spot_it: A cave mouth above a river, with a stream flowing out and bats in the dark beyond.
spotlights.story_md: Siju **Dobakkol**, the bat cave, sits by the Simsang river in the Garo Hills, near Napak Lake. It was explored by Stanley Kemp and K. Chopra of the Indian Museum in **1922**, one of the first scientific cave surveys in India, and became one of the best-studied caves in the subcontinent for its cave animals. Until 1981 it was India's longest known cave at 1.2 km; it is now surveyed at 4.77 km. Tens of thousands of bats live inside. Nearby Balpakram National Park has a canyon that Garo tradition holds is where spirits of the dead rest.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is where Indian cave biology began.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bats, blind animals and a 1922 survey: Siju.

sections.title: How Meghalaya earns, and what it costs
sections.intro_md:
Meghalaya's economy is small: a projected GSDP of about **₹76,300 crore** in 2026-27, and income per head of about **₹1.74 lakh**, which ranks near the bottom of Indian states, though poverty is lower than that suggests because land is held in common. Most people still farm: rice, maize, potato, ginger, turmeric, oranges, pineapple, areca nut and broom grass.

The rest comes from the ground. The Jaintia and Garo hills hold **coal** and some of India's best **limestone**, and the state's cement plants sit on it. For decades coal was dug by hand in **rat-hole** mines, narrow tunnels just big enough for a person to crawl, often by migrant and child workers. The National Green Tribunal **banned** such mining in **2014** after rivers ran acid and orange. Illegal mining did not stop.

The newer bets are **tourism**, which grew fast in the 2010s, hydropower, and industry at **Byrnihat** on the Assam border, which has brought jobs and some of the dirtiest air in the world.

spotlights.name: Rat-hole coal and the Ksan disaster
spotlights.spot_it: Black heaps beside small square pits on cleared hillsides, and orange-stained streams below.
spotlights.story_md: In rat-hole mining, a pit is dug down to a thin coal seam and then narrow horizontal tunnels, often under a metre high, are cut along it. Workers crawl in with picks. The National Green Tribunal banned the practice in 2014, citing acid drainage and deaths. On **13 December 2018**, at **Ksan** in East Jaintia Hills, miners in an illegal pit broke into an old flooded mine. Fifteen were trapped about 110 m down. Navy divers, Coal India and high-power pumps worked until March 2019, and only a few bodies were recovered. In January 2021 six more miners died in East Jaintia Hills.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the hidden cost of coal in a state that looks green from the road.
spotlights.memory_hook: A tunnel a metre high, 110 m down, and the water came in.

spotlights.name: Byrnihat
spotlights.when: World's most polluted city, IQAir 2024 report
spotlights.spot_it: Trucks, chimneys and dust on the Guwahati-Shillong highway where it crosses into Meghalaya.
spotlights.story_md: Byrnihat is an industrial town of steel, ferro-alloy and cement units straddling the Assam-Meghalaya border, about 14 km from Guwahati. In March 2025 the Swiss company **IQAir** ranked it the **most polluted city in the world** for 2024, with an average PM2.5 of **128.2 µg/m³**, about 25 times the World Health Organization guideline. Chief Minister Conrad Sangma disputed the figure, citing a state reading of about 50 µg/m³, and argued that units on the Assam side contribute. The state shut six units in early 2025. It is a sharp contrast to the 'abode of clouds' image.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that the state's growth model has a pollution problem.
spotlights.memory_hook: The cleanest-village state also hosts the dirtiest air on Earth.

sections.title: What is happening now (2025 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
**Languages, April 2026.** Through the Meghalaya Official Languages Ordinance, 2026, the state made **Khasi and Garo** full official languages alongside English. Khasi had been an associate official language in some districts since 2005. The demand to add both to the Constitution's Eighth Schedule continues.

**Air, March 2025.** IQAir's world report named **Byrnihat** the most polluted city on Earth for 2024. The state disputed the numbers and shut six units; the fight over who pollutes, Assam's side or Meghalaya's, continues.

**Tourism and safety, 2025.** In June 2025 the death of a honeymooning tourist near Sohra became national news, and the state stepped up guide registration and tourist safety rules in the Sohra trekking areas.

**Politics.** Conrad Sangma of the National People's Party, chief minister since March 2018, won a second term in March 2023 at the head of the Meghalaya Democratic Alliance. The next assembly election is due in early 2028.

**Every day.** DD News Meghalaya puts out bulletins in Khasi, Garo and English; the one embedded here is from 23 October 2026.

spotlights.name: Khasi and Garo become official languages
spotlights.spot_it: Government notices and signboards in Khasi and Garo, both in Roman script, beside English.
spotlights.story_md: For half a century English was Meghalaya's only official language, a choice made partly because no single local language united the state. In 2026 an ordinance made **Khasi and Garo** official too, after years of demands from students' unions and writers. It means government business, forms and courts can increasingly use the two main mother tongues. Both are written in Roman letters, Khasi in the system Thomas Jones began in 1841. Pnar speakers have asked for their language to be recognised as well.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It ends the oddity of a state whose two main languages had no official status.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fifty-four years after statehood, the state speaks its own languages officially.

sections.title: Myths, facts and recap
sections.intro_md:
**Myth: Cherrapunji is the wettest place on Earth.** It holds the records for the wettest year and the wettest month. On average, nearby Mawsynram is wetter, and two Colombian towns report even more.

**Myth: Meghalaya is a matriarchy.** It is matrilineal: names and property pass through women. Political power in the traditional system sat largely with men, and only three women won assembly seats in 2023.

**Myth: the root bridges are a natural wonder.** They are built. Each one is the work of generations of people training roots.

**Myth: everyone in Meghalaya speaks one tribal language.** Khasi and Garo come from two unrelated language families.

**Myth: the state is untouched wilderness.** It has rat-hole coal mines, acid streams and, in Byrnihat, the world's dirtiest air in 2024.

**Recap.** A plateau that catches the monsoon. Three matrilineal peoples. Stones for ancestors, bridges that grow, a Welsh alphabet and a whistled name. A state won by negotiation in 1972. Dance as worship, rock and choir as civic pride. And an economy still choosing between coal and clouds.

spotlights.name: The cautionary tale on every cliff
spotlights.spot_it: A signboard at every famous fall telling a story of grief, a demon or a lost giant.
spotlights.story_md: Almost every big landmark in Meghalaya has a story attached, told on boards to visitors and to children at home: Ka Likai's leap, the giant who carried Nartiang's stones, the ladder to heaven on Sohpetbneng, the spirit of the Mawphlang grove, Balpakram where the dead rest. These are not myths to be debunked. They are how a society without writing stored its rules about grief, greed, respect for forests and the clan. The best test is to ask what each story forbids.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Stories here do the work that laws and textbooks do elsewhere.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every cliff has a lesson; ask what it forbids.

best_facts.fact: Sohra (Cherrapunji) recorded 26,461 mm of rain between August 1860 and July 1861, still the world record for one year. Yet it runs short of drinking water every winter.
best_facts.why_surprising: Too much rain and too little water at the same address.

best_facts.fact: Everyone alive today lives in the 'Meghalayan Age', the geological unit for the last 4,200 years, defined by a stalagmite from a cave near Sohra.
best_facts.why_surprising: A small Indian state is printed on the global geological time scale.

best_facts.fact: Khasi villagers grow bridges: they train the roots of rubber fig trees across streams, a process taking 15 years or more, and the bridges get stronger with age.
best_facts.why_surprising: Infrastructure that is alive and improves over centuries.

best_facts.fact: In Kongthong, every child is given a whistled tune by its mother, used as a name to call them across the hills.
best_facts.why_surprising: A village where names are melodies.

best_facts.fact: In a Khasi family the youngest daughter, not the eldest son, inherits the ancestral house, and children take their mother's clan name.
best_facts.why_surprising: It inverts the default inheritance rule across most of India.

best_facts.fact: Khasi is related to Khmer, the language of Cambodia, while Garo, spoken in the same state, is related to Tibetan and Bodo.
best_facts.why_surprising: Neighbours in one small state speak languages from two families that split thousands of years ago.

best_facts.fact: Khasi is written in Roman letters because a Welsh missionary, Thomas Jones, chose them in 1841.
best_facts.why_surprising: An Indian language's alphabet traces back to rural Wales.

best_facts.fact: Every weekday in Shillong, the last two digits of the number of arrows that hit a target become a legal lottery number.
best_facts.why_surprising: An archery contest doubles as a daily betting game.

best_facts.fact: The 1897 earthquake lifted part of the Shillong Plateau by about 11 m along a single fault.
best_facts.why_surprising: One of the largest fault displacements ever measured happened under Shillong.

side_dish.title: Why mountains make rain: orographic lift
side_dish.body_md:
Air can only hold so much water vapour, and how much depends on temperature. Warm air holds a lot; cool air holds less. Push warm, wet air upward and it expands and cools, by roughly 6 to 10°C for every kilometre it rises. Once it cools to its dew point, the vapour condenses into droplets, droplets merge into drops, and it rains.

Mountains are the simplest way to push air up. Meteorologists call it **orographic lift**. During the south-west monsoon, air that has crossed the Bay of Bengal arrives over Bangladesh saturated. The plains are flat, so nothing lifts it. Then, at the Indian border, the Shillong Plateau rises like a wall. The air is forced up more than a kilometre in a short distance, and the plateau's southern lip around Sohra and Mawsynram gets the downpour. The funnel-shaped valleys there squeeze the air further.

The other side of the rule is the **rain shadow**. Air that has dropped its water on the windward slope sinks down the far side and warms, so it can hold its remaining moisture. That is why Shillong, only 50 km north of Sohra, gets around a fifth of Sohra's rain, and why Guwahati beyond is drier still. The same physics makes the Western Ghats' coast soaking and the Deccan dry, and makes Ladakh a desert behind the Himalaya.

offline_task.title: Cook a simple jadoh tonight
offline_task.body_md:
**Serves 3. 50 minutes. Pork is traditional; chicken thighs work.**

- 1 cup short-grain or red rice, washed and soaked 20 minutes
- 300 g pork with some fat (or chicken thighs), cut small
- 1 onion finely chopped, a 3 cm piece of ginger and 4 garlic cloves crushed
- 1 teaspoon turmeric (use Lakadong if you can find it), 2 bay leaves, salt, black pepper
- 1 tablespoon mustard oil or the pork's own fat

**Steps**
1. Heat the oil in a heavy pot. Brown the meat well, letting the fat run.
2. Add onion, ginger and garlic. Cook until soft.
3. Add turmeric, bay leaves, salt and pepper; stir for a minute.
4. Add the drained rice and stir so every grain is coated in fat.
5. Add 2 cups of water, bring to a boil, cover and cook on low for 18 to 20 minutes until the rice is soft.
6. Rest 5 minutes with the lid on.

Serve with a quick chutney of tomato, green chilli, onion and coriander. Notice the meat flavour soaked into every grain: that is the point of jadoh, a rice dish built to stretch a little pork across a whole family.
